questions.q: Why does this lesson say Salesforce's own platform-level protection isn't automatically a complete backup/recovery strategy for LTV Global?
options: Because it protects against platform-level failures, not against LTV Global's own mistakes like an accidental bulk update or a bad data load
Because Salesforce offers no data protection at all
Because backup/recovery is only relevant for Snowflake, not Salesforce
Because point-in-time recovery is impossible on any Salesforce org
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes platform-level protection from protection against LTV Global's own operational mistakes (bad bulk operations, mass updates), which is why a layered backup/recovery approach with point-in-time recovery is needed.

questions.q: What is point-in-time recovery, and why does it matter at LTV Global's scale?
options: Restoring data only to the most recent nightly export, regardless of when a problem occurred
A feature that prevents any bulk data operations from ever running
The ability to restore data to a specific past moment, which matters because an accidental bulk operation against millions of records is a realistic risk at this scale, not a hypothetical one
A monitoring feature unrelated to backup or recovery
questions.explain: Point-in-time recovery allows rolling back to a specific moment rather than losing everything since the last full export — important given the realistic risk of an accidental bulk operation against LTV Global's large-volume objects.

questions.q: What is the key difference between platform health monitoring and integration health monitoring, per this lesson?
options: There is no real difference; they monitor the same things

Platform health monitoring tracks Salesforce's own internal activity (logins, API usage), while integration health monitoring tracks whether external connections like the Meridian batch or LedgerPoint SFTP transfer completed successfully
Platform health monitoring only applies to EMEA
Integration health monitoring replaces the need for platform health monitoring entirely
questions.explain: The two monitoring layers track fundamentally different things — internal Salesforce activity versus the health of external-system connections — because failures in one wouldn't necessarily show up in the other.

questions.q: Why can't Salesforce's platform-health dashboard alone tell you that LedgerPoint's nightly batch silently failed?
options: Because platform-health dashboards are disabled for financial data
Because Salesforce does not support any kind of monitoring
Because LedgerPoint failures always trigger a Salesforce platform alert automatically
Because that failure happens entirely outside Salesforce, so only dedicated integration-health monitoring would catch it
questions.explain: LedgerPoint's batch process runs entirely outside Salesforce, so a Salesforce-only platform-health view has no visibility into whether that external batch succeeded — which is exactly the gap dedicated integration-health monitoring fills.

questions.q: How do Lesson 14's reconciliation step and Lesson 21's integration-health monitoring differ in what they catch?
options: Reconciliation catches data-level mismatches after a batch completes, while integration-health monitoring catches the batch not completing (or completing late) in the first place
They catch exactly the same problem and are fully redundant with each other
Reconciliation only applies to Meridian, while monitoring only applies to LedgerPoint
Monitoring replaces the need for reconciliation entirely
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes the two: reconciliation checks data accuracy after a batch finishes, while monitoring checks whether the batch ran and completed on time at all — neither substitutes for the other.
